1.0.0.en: 1- Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.

1.0.1.en: Blessed: O the happiness! In the Hebrew sense it takes a plural form, that is, an abundance of happiness and blessings.

1.0.2.en: 1- He praises the man who did not accept the counsel of the hypocrites, that is, the thought of the wicked, whether he rejected it from the beginning, or erred a little and accepted it, and then repented of it. He progresses from thought to conduct in the way of sinners, and this too the spiritual man rejected, whether from the beginning, or he stood in the way and then repented and departed from it. In the end sin grows greater and reaches settled abiding in it, for he says "sitteth", that is, the spiritual man refuses to settle in sin, and even if he falls he hastens to repent. The wicked man progresses from thought to conduct, and then to settling in sin. The spiritual man rejected all of these.

1.0.3.en: 2- Here he speaks symbolically about Christ, for He is the Man without sin who rejected the three degrees of sin.

1.0.4.en: 3- And if the meaning is a rebuke of Saul the wicked king, who progressed through the stages of sin, namely thought, then conduct, then settling, then he rebukes him by showing the greatness of the one who rejects all the degrees of sin, perhaps that he might repent. This is a great courtesy on the part of David, if he is the writer of the Psalm, because this Psalm was not given a title, and many incline to the view that its author is David, as we have mentioned.

1.1.0.en: 2- But his delight is in the law of the Lord; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.

1.1.1.en: 1- If he praised the spiritual man in (v. 1) for keeping away from evil, here he praises him for his positive conduct with regard to the law of the Lord. The law of the Lord means either the conscience, or the Law of Moses, which was a preparation for the law of Christ, that is, the Holy Bible and all the teachings of the Church.

1.1.2.en: 2- Here the importance of man's will and spiritual striving appears, in his inclination and desire to live by the law of the Lord. If human desire and readiness for striving are found, grace overflows to the man and helps him to carry out the commandments of the Lord.

1.1.3.en: 3- He affirms the importance of spiritual striving in his repetition, that is, his meditation on the words of the Lord, because repetition confirms the meaning within the mind, and then, when it takes hold of the thought, it easily leads the senses, speech and conduct.

1.1.4.en: 4- He declares that this meditation is day and night, that is, continually, that is, as long as he is awake, and in this state even his dreams are holy.

1.1.5.en: 5- Day and night signify the time of rest and the time of affliction, and they also signify the times of life with God and the times of falling into sin; in both cases the spiritual man must meditate on the word of God.

1.1.6.en: 6- Meditation on the word of God protects man from evil thoughts and draws him to heavenly things.

1.2.0.en: 3- And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.

1.2.1.en: 1- He compares the spiritual man to a tree planted by the rivers of water, and this water signifies the Holy Spirit, and the tree gives its fruit in its season, that is, at the right time of bearing fruit that those around it need. These fruits are the virtues with which the spiritual man is adorned and which influence those around him.

1.2.2.en: 2- In addition, the leaf of the tree does not wither, because the tree is filled with water, and its leaves are green and full of vitality, not dry so as to fall to the ground. The vitality of the leaf comes from the strong relationship with the Holy Spirit, who is the water. This leaf is the appearance of the tree, so it signifies the speech and appearance of the spiritual man; for his speech is from God, since the Holy Bible testifies that God gives His children from the Holy Spirit a mouth and wisdom (Lk 21:15). This speech is strong and firm and does not fall, ever influencing those around the spiritual man; indeed, his whole appearance influences those around him.

1.2.3.en: 3- Likewise all the works of this spiritual man are successful, because God works in him, and successful means that they lead to his salvation and the salvation of those around him, and material success is not what is meant, because material success is sometimes tied to evil.

1.2.4.en: 4- The tree can also signify Christ, planted by the rivers of water, that is, the Holy Spirit, who is His Spirit, and He gives His fruit, that is, salvation, in its season, that is, in the fullness of time He dies on the Cross, then rises on the third day, and founds His Church on the day of Pentecost. His leaf, that is, His word, is true and never falls, and everything He does is successful and leads to the salvation of mankind.

1.2.5.en: Take care that your words and deeds have a constructive aim that benefits you or benefits others. This is true success: that you draw near to God, or bring others near to God. As for words and deeds that have no aim, that is, that are vain, keep away from them.

1.3.0.en: 4- The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away.

1.3.1.en: Chaff: that is, straw, yellow in color.

1.3.2.en: Driveth away: that is, scatters it. The word is taken from the winnowing fork, an agricultural tool used to separate the grains of wheat from the straw.

1.3.3.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm shows the greatness of the spiritual man, who is compared to the tree planted by the rivers of water, by comparing him with the wicked, whom he likens to the opposite, that is, to light straw that is scattered by the wind far away so that it is found no more; he means the destruction of the wicked and their removal from God. But the spiritual man is firm in God.

1.3.4.en: 2- The wind signifies the trials that test the wicked, so they fall and depart from God. The wind also signifies pride, into which the wicked fall and which destroys them.

1.4.0.en: 5- Therefore the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous.

1.4.1.en: If the previous verse showed the wicked's departure from God on earth, then likewise in heaven, on the day of judgment, they will have no resurrection and no glorified life with Christ, but destruction will be theirs. Nor can sinners have a place among the righteous around Christ, because they will be cast into eternal torment.

1.5.0.en: 6- For the Lord knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish.

1.5.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm states in the end the sum of the matter, which is that God knows the way of the righteous, that is, He rejoices in them and they are with Him in the Kingdom, but the wicked, their portion is destruction, and they are far from the knowledge of God, meaning that they do not enjoy His love and His blessings of the Kingdom.

1.5.2.en: 2- God knows the obedience of His children to His commandments and rejoices in it, and then His joy is complete if they complete their life on earth, and He gives them everlasting glory and complete joy with Him in heaven.

1.5.3.en: Be careful to memorize and repeat the words of the Holy Bible, so that they keep you in all your ways, and in this way God is in your mind and with you always, and you enjoy fellowship with Him on earth until your joy is made complete in heaven. Christ the King and the enmity of the nations "Why do the heathen rage" ... (v. 1) Introduction:

1.5.4.en: 1- Its writer: the prophet David, because the Apostles Peter and John ascribed it to him (Acts 4:25).

1.5.5.en: 2- This Psalm is considered one of the Messianic Psalms, that is, those that speak about Christ the awaited Messiah, and it is considered one of the royal Psalms because it speaks about King David, who is a type of Christ.

1.5.6.en: 3- And while the first Psalm speaks about man's choice of his way, if he chooses life with God, it requires that he believe in Christ the Savior, who gives him the new life in Him on earth and the Kingdom of Heaven.

1.5.7.en: 4- The content of this Psalm is the sufferings of Christ, the world's rising up against Him, and His endurance of everything for the sake of our salvation, and how He conquered Satan and gave us authority over him, and the call to mankind, with all its great ones, to submit to Christ.

1.5.8.en: 5- This Psalm is found in the Prime prayer of the Agpeya.

2.0.s.en: (1) The nations' rising up against the Lord's Anointed

2.0.0.en: 1- Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?

2.0.1.en: Rage: gathered together and assembled for war.

2.0.2.en: 1- This Psalm begins with a question that David asks of God, to know the reason for the rising up of the nations of the earth and the peoples against the awaited Messiah, for he sees with the eye of prophecy the rising up of the Jews and of the Roman state, which ruled the world, against Christ until they crucified Him.

2.0.3.en: 2- He also asks about the nations' rising up against King David, who is a type of Christ, although God gave David victory over all the nations around him, and this appeared in his successive victories over the nations, so the rest of the nations ought to have submitted to him, and not tried to rise up against him or fight him.

2.0.4.en: 3- He describes the thoughts of these peoples and their plots as vain, that is, without benefit.

2.0.5.en: 4- This question may be one of astonishment and denunciation, as he asks how the nations and peoples dared to fight the Lord of glory Jesus, who has authority over everything, so the Jews fabricated false, lying and vain accusations against Christ Jesus. And the wonder is that they imagine a vain thing in killing the Source of life. Or how can it occur to him to fight King David, whom God supports, so that no one can overcome him? Consequently all their plots are vain.

2.0.6.en: 5- This question may also be a rebuke, that is, David rebukes the nations and peoples for their insolence and daring to rise up against the Lord's anointed, that is, David, or the awaited Messiah; they have forgotten their weakness and the power of God who is before them.

2.1.0.en: 2- The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord, and against his anointed, saying,

2.1.1.en: Kings of the earth: Herod, who killed the children of Bethlehem, and Pilate, who crucified Christ.

2.1.2.en: The rulers: the chief priests and elders of the Jewish people.

2.1.3.en: The Psalmist continues his question about the daring of the rulers of God's people and the kings of the world, that they should try to destroy Christ and crucify Him. He affirms that these plots are not against the person of Jesus the man, who appeared before them in weakness, but against God, because He is God incarnate. Their plotting against David is also against God, who supports and protects him, for David is the Lord's anointed, that is, anointed with oil as king by the Lord, and is not like the rest of the kings of the earth, so whoever opposes him opposes God.

2.2.0.en: 3- "Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us."

2.2.1.en: 1- The nations hostile to God cried out in rejection of His authority and of following Him, accusing Him that following Him lays on them heavy bonds and cords. In the Septuagint it says "fetters and a yoke"; the fetters are the bonds, and the yoke is the wooden beam that is placed on the necks of animals to pull farm implements behind them.

2.2.2.en: 2- Although the yoke of Christ is easy and His burden is light (Mt 11:30), His commandments give rest to the soul and bring it salvation, whereas the bonds of sin and the lusts of the world humiliate man and lead him to destruction.

2.2.3.en: Do not be troubled by the plotting of the wicked or of anyone who threatens you, for they are worth nothing before the power of God that supports you. Only hold fast to God's commandments and remain firm in His Church.

2.3.0.en: 4- He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision.

2.3.1.en: 1- God who dwells in the heavens laughs at the plots of the wicked, because they are worth nothing and do not hinder His salvation, which He offers to the world on the Cross; on the contrary, He turns their plots into a means of saving the world. By His death for mankind, they kill Him and He redeems them; they bury Him and He draws them to heaven: "And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me" (Jn 12:32).

2.3.2.en: 2- The heavens can also be the souls of God's children and His saints, in whom He dwells because of their conduct being exalted above the world, for He is glorified in His saints, and the plots of the wicked fail to stop their relationship with Him; on the contrary, all the sufferings and torments they are subjected to make them cling to Him. And by their death for His sake they receive the crowns of martyrdom and the crowns of striving and service.

2.3.3.en: 3- God derides the plots of the wicked in the world, for they are nothing before His power. The attempts of the scribes and Pharisees to ensnare Christ in a word showed His wisdom and power and at the same time their weakness. And when they crucified Christ and He died, He rose and gave His disciples, who were simple and ignorant in the eyes of the world, power, and they preached in His name and drew many in the whole world to Him. Thus God derides the false wisdom of this world and its vain power, and faith in Him spreads in the midst of tribulations and persecutions.

2.4.0.en: 5- Then shall he speak unto them in his wrath, and vex them in his sore displeasure.

2.4.1.en: Vex them: makes them tremble with fear.

2.4.2.en: After the Lord has laughed at them and derided them, He shows His wrath against them by rebuking them, as He rebuked the scribes and Pharisees and pronounced woes on them (Mt 23). But if they refuse to submit to Him through repentance, He frightens them and makes them tremble with His severe punishment of them, as He allowed the Romans to destroy Jerusalem and kill thousands of Jews in AD 70. And as all the wicked will tremble before Him on the day of judgment, and then He casts them into eternal torment.

2.4.3.en: The opportunity of life is for repentance and for enjoying the tenderness of God, even if it appears in the form of strong commandments or severe warnings. All this protects us from eternal punishment and destruction. May we not refuse God's hand stretched out to us every day to return to Him.

2.5.s.en: (3) Christ the King, the Son of G

2.5.0.en: 6- "Yet have I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion."

2.5.1.en: 1- Here he speaks about God, who anointed David king over Israel and took as his capital Jerusalem, which is Zion.

2.5.2.en: 2- God, the King of kings and Lord of lords, the eternal and everlasting, became incarnate in the fullness of time. The Father declares that Jesus Christ His Son He anointed in the Jordan on the day of His Baptism as King in Zion, that is, Jerusalem, the holy hill of God, where His great temple is, and it is a type of the Church, over which Christ was anointed King and Redeemer of all mankind. He called it the hill of His holiness because the temple is built on a hill, which signifies the loftiness of God's temple, and a type of the Church, which is the icon of heaven on earth, and the Church is built on the rock, which is Christ (Mt 16:18), just as the temple is built on the hill.

2.5.3.en: 3- Christ was called King because the Magi offered Him among their gifts gold, because He is a king, and He spoke of Himself at the end of days, saying, "Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand" (Mt 25:34). And He confirmed the words of Pilate when he asked Him whether He was a king, and He said to him, "Thou sayest" (Jn 18:37); so He is a king, indeed the King of kings.

2.6.0.en: 7- I will declare the decree: the Lord hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee.

2.6.1.en: The Psalmist David announces news concerning what God has decreed, namely the Incarnation of the Son in the fullness of time, to redeem mankind, and here he declares two things:

2.6.2.en: 1- "Thou art my Son", that is, the hypostasis of the Father says of the Second Hypostasis that He is My Son. And He also says, "this day have I begotten thee", and "this day" represents the permanent present, that is, the Son is begotten of the Father from eternity and to eternity.

2.6.3.en: 2- He speaks about the Incarnation, for by "this day" he also means the fullness of time in which Christ became incarnate for the salvation of mankind. And He said "begotten thee" and not "created thee", because He is begotten, not created, of one essence with the Father, as we say in the Creed.

2.6.4.en: 3- This verse also applies to David: although the people asked for a king instead of God and He set Saul over them according to what pleased them in outward appearance, after this He sets over them a king who is a true son of God, whose heart is like the heart of God, and he is David. So He declares that he was begotten today, whether He means the day of his birth, or the day of his being anointed king by the hand of Samuel.

2.7.0.en: 8- Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.

2.7.1.en: 1- The Father calls the Son, saying to Him, ask of Me and I will give You the nations of the world as an inheritance and a possession, however far away, even to the ends of the earth. The Father means that all that is His He gives to the Son (Jn 16:15), and this was accomplished when Christ died on the Cross and paid the debt for mankind, to save everyone who believes in Him and lives with Him.

2.7.2.en: 2- By "Ask of me" he also means that there is a constant dialogue between the Son and the Father, that is, within the Divine Essence. If limited man has within his mind a stream of thoughts and dialogues, how much more so within the Divine Essence.

2.7.3.en: 3- This verse shows the extent of love and unity among the hypostases.

2.7.4.en: 4- "Ask of me" does not mean that there is incomplete knowledge or lesser power in the Son that He wants to receive and learn from the Father, but, as we said, it is an expression of dialogue, love and unity within the Divine Essence among the hypostases.

2.7.5.en: 5- If we apply this verse to David, it applies only partially, for the kingdom of Israel in the days of David became as wide as it could be, and God's promise was fulfilled, which He made to the fathers, that He would give them the land from the river Euphrates to the river of Egypt, which is a seasonal river of torrents lying in the wilderness of Sinai. This did not happen except in the days of David and not before him.

2.8.0.en: 9- Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel.

2.8.1.en: 1- Christ is the King of kings, and the king has the scepter of kingship with which he shepherds his people, and because those who oppose Christ are created from clay, that is, weak human beings, He says of them that they are a potter's vessels, that is, vessels made of pottery.

2.8.2.en: 2- And when He breaks them and shatters them, they turn into useless pieces, but if they repent He reshapes them and makes them vessels of honor and glory.

2.8.3.en: 3- But if they insist on resisting Him, He punishes them with eternal torment on the day of judgment.

2.8.4.en: 4- The meaning of this is that the scepter of Christ's kingship contains mercy and justice together: whoever responds to Him with repentance receives mercy, and whoever insists on his sins deserves justice.

2.8.5.en: We are children of God and have boldness to ask Him for our needs and for the forgiveness of our sins; as the Son asks of the Father, He encourages us to ask of God and to rejoice in His love and gifts.

2.9.0.en: 10- Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth.

2.9.1.en: 1- David the king and judge calls the kings of the earth to walk in reason and wisdom, so that they believe in Christ the Savior and keep His commandments, and likewise the judges, to walk in discipline and good conscience, that is, to judge with justice, and so submit to the just God and His holy Christ.

2.9.2.en: 2- And when the king and judge are wise and instructed, it influences his people and followers, so David by this calls the leaders to bring the peoples to faith in Christ and submission to Him.

2.9.3.en: 3- Every spiritual man is considered a king and ruler over himself (Rev 1:6) and a judge, with justice, over his actions when he examines himself every day, for every believer who knows God's commandments passes God's judgment on himself before others. That is, David calls every man to submit to Christ and keep His commandments and live with discipline and reason.

2.10.0.en: 11- Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling.

2.10.1.en: The prophet David continues his speech to the kings and judges, to call them to serve God with fear, that is, to offer repentance with contrition and tears before God, knowing that it is a great grace that God allows them, despite the multitude of their sins, to come before Him and serve Him, offering prayers of reverence before the King of kings and Lord of lords. He also calls them to rejoice, or to exult as the Septuagint (the Agpeya) says, with trembling before God. This means that they will rejoice in being in the presence of God, so they lift up their voices with shouting and exultation, but at the same time this joy is mixed with trembling, that is, they do not lose their fear and reverence before God, for they rejoice in their sonship to God, which He has bestowed on them although, because of the multitude of their sins, they do not deserve to be servants to Him. This is true repentance, bound up with bent knees, tears and contrite prayers, so the heart is filled with joy and consolation at the same time.

2.11.0.en: 12- Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him.

2.11.1.en: 1- It was an ancient custom among peoples to declare their submission to the king by kissing his feet; therefore the Psalmist calls the kings and judges to kiss the Son, that is, to kiss His feet and submit to Him and keep His commandments. For if they do not submit, the wrath of God, that is, His punishment, awaits them, and this is not an emotional passion like that of human beings but His divine judgment on those who oppose Him, so they are cast into eternal torment for their insistence on sin. And this torment is what he calls perishing from the way, that is, from the life, that is, the Kingdom.

2.11.2.en: 2- The Psalmist also warns that God's wrath is soon to be kindled, that is, the day of judgment, when Christ judges everyone who refused to believe in Him and did not keep His commandments. Therefore the Church has lived since its beginning in the apostolic age preparing for the day of judgment by repentance and spiritual striving, and if at times she grows weak and forgets this eschatological dimension, God alerts her through tribulations to return to the power of the age of the Apostles.

2.11.3.en: 3- At the end of the Psalm the prophet David pronounces blessed the children of God who trust in Him, that is, those who believe in Him and keep His commandments. And as the first Psalm begins with a beatitude, the second Psalm also ends with a beatitude for the children of God, to encourage them to live with Him.

2.11.4.en: God's arms are open to you if you are repentant and reject your sins. However weak you are, and even if you accepted sin by your own will and even took pleasure in it, and then awoke after tasting the bitterness of the fall, return quickly with fear and tears, and you will receive mercies and consolations from God in the sacrament of confession that cannot be expressed. The salvation of the Lord A Psalm of David when he fled from the face of Absalom his son "Lord, how are they increased that trouble me" ... (v. 1) Introduction:

2.11.5.en: 1- Its writer: the prophet and king David, when his son Absalom rose up against him to kill him, and he fled barefoot from Jerusalem and was suffering feelings of grief; for how hard it is when children rebel and rise up against their parents to harm them, even trying to kill them. This Psalm is also considered one of the Messianic Psalms, because it clearly prophesies the sufferings of Christ, His death and His resurrection, for example it says in (v. 5), "I laid me down and slept; I awaked."

2.11.6.en: 2- This Psalm suits everyone who suffers pains, persecutions and frustrations from those around him, so his hope in God his Savior is renewed.

2.11.7.en: 3- The Fathers consider the first and second Psalms an introduction to the Book of Psalms, as the first speaks about life with God and keeping away from evil, and the second Psalm declares clearly that this life is accomplished only through Christ the Savior and submission to His commandments.

2.11.8.en: 4- As for this third Psalm, it suits everyone who begins his day with prayer, for after he lies down and sleeps he rises with Christ and awakes, relying on God his Helper. It is followed by the fourth Psalm, which many of the Fathers see as suitable for prayer at the end of the day, because it says "commune with your own heart upon your bed" and also says "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep." Therefore the Church arranged that the fourth Psalm be repeated in the prayer of the Veil, which is said at the end of the day.

2.11.9.en: 5- The third Psalm is also repeated and said in the First Watch of the Midnight prayer, because it contains "I laid me down and slept; I awaked", and this is what happens with one who prays at midnight.

2.11.10.en: 6- Some of the Fathers consider this Psalm a personal lament of David, in which he pours out his sorrows and pains over the rising up of Absalom his son against him.
